bracket: [Textbook answer-key error, and it is self-refuting on the stem's own \(K_p\). The key prints \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 0.96\,\text{bar}\). That value is not the hydrogen pressure — it is what is LEFT of each reactant: solving \(x/(4.0-x) = \sqrt{10.1} = 3.178\) gives \(x = 3.0426\), and \(4.0 - 3.0426 = 0.9574 \approx 0.96\). Taking the key at face value inverts the equilibrium: with \(p_{\text{H}_2} = p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.9574\) and \(p_{\text{CO}} = p_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 3.0426\), the constant comes out \(0.0990 = 1/10.1\) — the RECIPROCAL of the \(K_p\) the question supplies. The answer below substitutes back to \(10.100\).]

[Textbook answer-key error: the key lists \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) as a Lewis acid alongside \(\text{BF}_3\) and \(\text{H}^{+}\). A Lewis acid must ACCEPT an electron pair, which requires either an incomplete octet or a vacant low-energy orbital. In \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) the nitrogen already has a complete octet with all four pairs used in bonding, no lone pair left over and no vacant valence orbital, so it can neither donate nor accept a pair. The chapter's own \(\S 6.10.3\) illustrates Lewis acids with ELECTRON-DEFICIENT species, which is exactly what \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) is not. Worth knowing why the error is tempting: \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) IS a BRONSTED acid, since it can give up a proton — but that is a different definition, and under the Lewis definition the species that accepts the electron pair is the \(\text{H}^{+}\) released, not the ammonium ion itself.]

[Textbook answer-key error — the key answers a different question from the one asked. It prints \(2.5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{M}\), which is exactly \(\sqrt{K_{sp}} = 2.510 \times 10^{-9}\), i.e. the ion concentration AFTER the two solutions are mixed. The question asks for the concentration of the solutions that are then mixed in equal volumes, and mixing equal volumes halves each concentration, so the solutions may be twice as concentrated: \(5.02 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{M}\). The chapter applies that same dilution correctly in Ex 6.69 and Ex 6.73, which is what makes this a slip rather than a convention. Both values are named here because a reader who takes "the solution" to mean the mixture will arrive at the key's figure, and because an examiner following the book will expect it.]

[Textbook answer-key error of OMISSION: the key names only \(\text{CdCl}_2\) as precipitating, and \(\text{ZnCl}_2\) does too. Taking \(K_{sp}(\text{ZnS}) = 1.6 \times 10^{-24}\) from the chapter's own Table 6.9, the ionic product for the zinc solution works out at \(8.89 \times 10^{-22}\) — larger than \(K_{sp}\) by a factor of about 556, so zinc sulphide is well past saturation. The conclusion does not depend on how the dilution on mixing is treated: ignoring it gives an ionic product of \(4 \times 10^{-21}\), larger still. The answer below names both salts.]
